title: Film Slide Collage: SCRAP Creative Reuse

They are prefect to take home and give out to friends. –All materials provided, sourced from SCRAP’s reuse stock –Step-by-step help from our EDU team –A finished diy to take home –Warm-up-your-home vibes and good company Carol Taite, the volunteer educator teaching this workshop, is a local artist who has been sourcing from SCRAP for many years. Her personal creative projects include garment making and whimsical textile art. 12pm-2pm | Ages 16+. Reserve your seats before the event! Drop-in is not guaranteed. ————————– SCRAP prioritizes access to affordable art materials and expression, so we’re offering tiered ticket options: Independent Crafter ($8) – This ticket reflects the “true value” of the event and is geared toward those who will be creating solo or with assistance from an adult. All event ticket sales are final and non-refundable. Questions on the day of the event? Don’t hesitate to call the store (734-800-4137). If you cannot make it to the event, feel free to send a friend in your place— we’d love to host them! Thank you for understanding and supporting our SCRAPpy little creative reuse non-profit.

On Sat. & Sun., staffers show some native Michigan animals, including a cougar, black rat snake, and opossum a t 1 & 4 p.m.; and a wild turkey at 2 & 3 p.m. During the Friday Adult Open Hours (age 18+ only), conservancy staffers show all four animals at 7:30 p.m. All tickets include a chance to see the conservancy’s other animals. description: Every Sat. & Sun., except Nov. 15, 28, & 29. Hands-on 20-minute family-oriented demo for age 5 & up that explores magnetism, magnetic fields, and what they have to do with everyday life. 12:30 & 2:30 p.m., 1105 North University. Free. (734) 764–0478, ummnh.org.

description: Every Fri.–Sun. Three different audiovisual planetarium shows suitable for all ages. Did an Asteroid Really Kill the Dinosaurs? (noon) looks at cosmic collisions across the solar system including the 6-mile-wide asteroid that hit the earth 66 million years ago; The Sky Tonight (1 & 3 p.m.) explores the current night sky, with tips on how to find the cardinal directions, constellations, and planets on your own; and T. Rex (2 p.m.) describes the iconic dinosaur’s scientific and cinematic history (includes scenes of dinosaur violence). Noon, 1, 2, & 3 p.m., 1105 North University. $9 at the gift shop. Limited capacity. (734) 764–0480, ummnh.org.

title: Drop-in Knitting: Spun
description: Every Sun.–Thurs. (different times). All invited to work on their knitting, crochet, weaving, and embroidery projects. 1–3 p.m. (Sun.) & 6–8 p.m. (Mon.–Thurs.), 401 N. Fourth Ave. Free. (734) 780–7867.

title: Letterpress Open Lab: Ann Arbor District Library
description: Nov. 3, 8, 16, & 22 (different times). A chance for adults to learn the basics of printing with movable type. 5–7 p.m. (Nov. 3 & 16), noon–2 p.m. (Nov. 8), and 1–3 p.m. (Nov. 22), AADL Downtown, Secret Lab. Free. (734) 327–4200.

title: Black Washtenaw County & the Civil War: Motorcoach & Walking Tour
description: Visit the sites connected to Black Civil War veterans who called Washtenaw County home. Historians Deborah Meadows and Matthew Siegfried will lead visitors on a motorcoach and walking journey through Ann Arbor and Ypsilanti including historic Black neighborhoods, Depot Town, and Highland Cemetery, the final resting place of at least 19 Black Civil War soldiers. This tour is presented in conjunction with the Frankel Detroit Observatory’s exhibit, “Fill the Ranks”: The Civil War and the University of Michigan, and is offered in partnership with the African American Cultural and Historical Museum of Washtenaw County. Free and open to the public. Limited availability; registration required.

title: The Art of Sashiko: Rescue Rose
description: If you’ve ever mourned the loss of a favorite garment due to wear and tear, this decorative hand-stitching workshop is for you! Discover the Japanese tradition of Sashiko, the art of functional and decorative fabric repair, taught by skilled sewist Chelsea Keenan. Sessions will take place on Saturday November 21 from 1-4, and Sunday November 22 from 1-4. Participants will bring one garment with a repair area smaller than 6×6 inches. All other necessary materials will be provided. The cost of the workshop is $30, plus Eventbrite fees. Limited space is available, please sign up here: https://www.eventbrite.com/e/sashiko-the-japanese-art-of-visible-mending-tickets-2000903471145

title: “Growing Genealogy’s Future: Attracting and Engaging Younger People”: Genealogical Society of Washtenaw County
description: Talk, via Zoom on a big screen, by genealogist Sarah Day. Followed by small group discussions (in person and on Zoom) on the same topic, as well as on genealogy research questions. 1:30–4:30 p.m., Trinity Health Education Center Auditorium, 5305 Elliott, parking lot P, Ypsi. Also via livestream; for URL email info@washtenawgenealogy.org by Nov. 20. Free. washtenawgenealogy.org/events.

title: “Walking with Whales Tour”: U-M Museum of Natural History
description: Nov. 1, 8, & 22. Thirty-minute tour that uses the museum’s specimens to tell the story of prehistoric whales and dolphins, who had 4 limbs and walked on land. 1:30 p.m., 1105 North University. Free. Limited capacity. Sign up at the welcome desk. (734) 764–0478.

title: “Bastard”: Purple Rose Theatre Company
description: Every Wed.–Sun., Sept. 24–Dec. 20. Rhiannon Ragland directs retired Detroit newscaster and playwright Devin Scillian’s family comedy-drama about a conflict between brothers—an aging country rocker and a buttoned-down finance guy—after their mother’s death. Adult language and subject matter. 7:30 p.m. (Thurs.), 8 p.m. (Fri. & Sat.), 2 p.m. (Sun.), & 3 p.m. (Sat. & Wed.). 137 Park St., Chelsea. Tickets $31.50–$52.50 in advance at purplerosetheatre.org, (734) 433–7673, & (if available) at the door. Discounts available.

title: Exhibition Tour: “We Hold These Truths” with Dean Celeste Watkins-Hayes
description: Join Dean Celeste Watkins-Hayes and award-winning artist Holly Bass for a tour of “We Hold These Truths”. 🗓️ Sunday, Nov 22 ⏰ 2-3 PM 📍UMMA 🎟️ Free & open to the public: registration required. “We Hold These Truths” marks the return of visitors to UMMA’s iconic Lizzie and Jonathan Tisch Apse following a nearly year-long restoration of its signature marble floor, transforming the storied space into a sequence of encounters with rooms, replicas, and acts of writing that move through the nation’s past and present.

title: ​​Ari Axelrod: Kerrytown Concert House
description: See 19 Thursday. Today, Axelrod reprises his program, L’chaim!, performed at KCH in March 2026. Built around songs that give him chills and celebrate the gift of life, the program blends Broadway, Jewish, and international music. 2–4 p.m.

title: Michigan Youth Jazz Orchestra: U-M Music School
description: Dennis Wilson directs high school students from around the state in a program of big band jazz standards. 2 p.m., U-M Moore Bldg. Hankinson Rehearsal Hall, 1100 Baits. Free. (734) 764–0538.

description: All invited to listen to guild members swap stories or bring their own to tell. Note different location for just this month. 2–4 p.m., Trinity Lutheran Church, 1400 W. Stadium. Free. annarborstorytelling.org.

description: Nov. 20 –Dec. 6, except Nov. 26. Lauren London directs local actors in local playwright Michael Alan Herman’s existential fantasy comedy-drama about a pair of elderly farmers who farm clouds for their silver linings as they struggle to keep their farm—and their relationship—intact. 8 p.m. (Thurs.–Sat.) & 2 p.m. (Sun.). Cahoots, 206 E. Huron St. Tickets $28 (students, $20; seniors, $25), in advance at pennyseats.org & (if available) at the door. (734) 926 – 5346 , thepennyseats@gmail.com.

description: Nov. 20–22. Gonzalo Delgado directs fellow U-M students in Arthur Laurents’ spirited musical adaptation of Romeo and Juliet, set in New York and featuring the rival street gangs the Sharks and the Jets. The beloved Leonard Bernstein–Stephen Sondheim score includes such favorites as “Maria,” “Tonight,” and “America.” 7:30 p.m. (Fri. & Sat.) & 2 p.m. (Sun.), Power Center. Tickets $15 (students and kids age 12 & under, $9) in advance at ummusket.org & at the door. musket.prod@umich.edu.

description: Nov. 20–22. Members of this local theater troupe perform Lauren Gunderson’s 2015 biographical drama, a fictionalized retelling of the story of the 1926 Nobel Prize–nominated Harvard astronomer Henrietta Leavitt. 7 p.m. (Fri. & Sat.) & 2 p.m. (Sat. & Sun.), Columbus Hall, 8265 Dexter-Chelsea Rd., Dexter. Tickets $20 (students & seniors, $15) in advance at dcp.yapsody.com & at the door.

title: “Gross Indecency: The Three Trials of Oscar Wilde”: U-M Theatre Department
description: Nov. 19–22. Halena Kays directs drama students in Moisés Kaufman’s award-winning 1997 play that chronicles the swift and tragic downfall of the famous Irish playwright. Wilde sued the Marquess of Queensberry in 1895 for criminal libel after the Marquess called him a “posing sodomite.” This lawsuit backfired on Wilde, resulting in two additional trials to determine whether he was guilty of “gross indecency with male persons.” Recommended for ages 16 & up. 7:30 p.m. (Thurs.), 8 p.m. (Fri. & Sat.), & 2 p.m. (Sun.), Lydia Mendelssohn Theatre, 911 North University. Tickets $29–$35 (students, $16) in advance at tickets.smtd.umich.edu & at the door. (734) 764–0538.

title: “Jack Tucker Comedy Standup Show”: University Musical Society
description: Nov. 18–22. New York City cult favorite Zach Zucker, a French-trained comedic performer known for blending clowning with satire, appears as Tucker, a dim, delusional, and overconfident hack stand-up whose desperate need to be adored drives him to the brink of comedy chaos. With an absurdist sound design fueling the unraveling, the result is a “raucously funny” “triumph” according to the New York Times reviewer, who says “not since The Play That Goes Wrong have I seen mistakes this meticulous.” Age 14 & up. 7:30 p.m. (Wed.–Sat.) & 2 p.m. (Sun.), Arthur Miller Theatre, 1226 Murfin. $36–$46 (students, $15–$20). (734) 764–2538, ums.org.

description: Jacob Carroll directs this women’s early-music choir in a program that juxtaposes English choral music of the Renaissance with the medieval-era music of the Notre Dame school of polyphony. Works include John Dunstable’s Magnificat, John Taverner’s Missa Playnsong, and a selection of Gregorian chants dedicated to holy women. Also, the premiere of four short pieces composed for the Grail Singers by Nora Farley, with text from the Sappho fragments. Accompaniment by Abigail Petersen on chamber organ. 4 p.m., St. Andrew’s Episcopal Church, 306 N. Division. Tickets $20 (seniors, $15; students, $10) at annarborgrailsingers.org & (if available) by cash or check at the door. (415) 662–0631, annarborgrailsingers.org.

Followed by a chance to make a didukh, a sheaf of wheat, which symbolizes ancestral memory, hope, and abundant harvest, and a moment of silence to honor the victims of the Holodomor genocide. 5 p.m. AADL Downtown, 3rd fl.

title: For parents:  “Harnessing the power of talking out loud”
description: It happens so often. You’re talking to your child and something you say causes a disconnection, and your child checks out. What becomes possible instead if you offer to be a “teddy bear?” Teddy bears say very little. When a teddy bear does talk, it is because the talker has asked the teddy bear to do something small, like ask questions or reflect some things back. When a teddy bear asks a question, the question isn’t about any concerns or agenda that the teddy bear might have. Instead, the question is open and honest and supports the talker in having plenty of room to take things where the talker wants to go. In this workshop, we will explore open, honest questions and many more aspects of Teddy Bear Talk Support.

title: Harnessing the power of talking out loud workshop
description: Do you think better when thinking out loud? Learn how to set things up using Teddy Bear Talk Support so that you can clear the way for the power of listening to work its magic more effectively. Teddy Bear Talk Support provides a framework for benefiting from listeners who say very little. We’ll call these listeners teddy bears. When a teddy bear does talk, it is because the talker has asked the teddy bear to do something small, like ask some open, honest questions or reflect some things back. Big changes can happen for the talker as a result of the little things the teddy bear might do or say to just “jiggle” things a bit for the talker.
